stories.headline: Denver and Littleton sue Bow Mar over gate and road closure project
stories.summary:
Denver and Littleton filed a joint lawsuit Monday in Denver District Court against the town of Bow Mar. The suit seeks to stop construction of a gate at South Sheridan Boulevard and the planned closure of West Tufts Avenue at the town line. The cities argue the barriers exceed Bow Mar's authority under state law.

The lawsuit says the gates close roads the Colorado Department of Transportation classifies as major collectors, which the regional transportation system relies on. It argues the gates are not a reasonable exercise of police power and would shift traffic and potential collisions onto neighboring cities. Mayor Mike Johnston said Bow Mar does not get to decide what is or isn't a public road, and Littleton Mayor Kyle Schlachter called for equal access for residents of both cities.

Bow Mar, a community of about 900 residents, has said it expects the Sheridan gate to be erected by the end of the month and operational by January. Only residents, emergency services and delivery trucks could open it. Town data show roughly 1,200 vehicles enter via Sheridan daily, up 51% over eight years, and police have issued nearly 900 citations for speeding and unsafe driving in four years. A town spokesman had no immediate comment.

stories.headline: Jeffco Public Schools' $73 million measure fails by five votes, headed toward recount
stories.summary:
Jeffco Public Schools Ballot Issue 5A, which would raise $73 million, was failing by just five votes out of 301,789 cast as of Monday. The district is waiting for overseas ballots to be counted by Friday, and the narrow margin is expected to trigger an automatic recount. The recount threshold is 754 votes, or 0.5% of the race leader's total.

If a recount occurs, results will not be official until Dec. 4, according to district spokeswoman Devra Ashby. If 5A passes, the money would go toward employee salaries and expanded career and technical programs. A second override, Ballot Issue 5B, would have raised $60 million for building maintenance and was failing by 7,563 votes.

The district recently cut $45 million from its budget, including 139 jobs, and expects a deficit of at least $13 million in the 2027-28 school year if 5A fails. Interim Superintendent Rob Stein said Jeffco's per-pupil funding lags neighboring districts and that it has relied less on overrides. Denver voters approved a nearly $44 million override for Denver Public Schools, while a $54 million measure failed in Douglas County.

stories.headline: 34% of Colorado households are cost-burdened, state housing study finds
stories.summary:
A statewide housing needs assessment released Monday found that nearly 34% of Colorado households spent more than 30% of their income on housing as of July 1. That includes 49% of renters and 25% of homeowners, and the share rises as income falls. Colorado tends to have a higher share of cost-burdened households than other states, according to separate Harvard research.

The State Demography Office produced the first assessment under 2024 legislation requiring analysis of current housing stock and estimated needs over the next decade. A household needs to earn $153,000 a year to afford the median-priced home of $547,900, and renters need $72,900 to afford the average apartment. The gap between income and what is needed to buy an average home is about $50,000, compared with $2,600 in 2013.

Over the past three years home prices have been relatively stable and incomes have risen slowly, narrowing the gap. The report arrives as a new governor and Legislature take power in January. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser has set a goal of adding 40,000 affordable units by 2035 through measures such as down payment assistance and permitting reform.

stories.headline: Business groups warn graduated income tax will burden small businesses
stories.summary:
The National Federation of Independent Business called passage of Amendment 87 disappointing for Colorado's small business owners and taxpayers. The measure replaces the state's flat 4.4% income tax with a graduated rate that raises taxes on those earning $500,000 or more, while lower earners see a decrease of a few hundred dollars.

NFIB's Michael Smith said higher taxes force owners to raise prices, cut hours, stop hiring or eliminate jobs. The Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce's Leslie Oliver said small businesses may have to cut pay, safety investments and savings. Amendment 87 is expected to raise at least $2 billion, with some estimates at $2.7 billion, to be spent on K-12 and higher education, health care and child care.

The measure needed only a simple majority because it touched a small provision of TABOR. A competing measure to cap the rate at 4.4% received 47%. Supporters in the Protect Colorado's Future coalition said the ultra-wealthy and corporations will pay their fair share.

stories.headline: Centro Mexican Kitchen closing in Boulder to make way for Altura
stories.summary:
Centro Mexican Kitchen will close Nov. 14 after 20 years at 950 Pearl St. in Boulder. The space will become Altura, a new Mountain Mexican restaurant from Big Red F founder Dave Query, opening Dec. 8 after a soft renovation.

Planned upgrades include a 16-foot folding glass wall opening to Pearl Street, new floors, booths, chairs and lighting, structural updates, whitewashed walls and removal of the large colorful mural. Query said the menu will remain Mexican but be reevaluated, with more attention to flavors and presentation. Big Red F Culinary Director Sheila Lucero and chef Jason Schmid will work on the menu.

Big Red F, which began operating in Colorado in 1994, owns 12 restaurants and bars along the Front Range. The same corner previously housed Rhumba, another Big Red F restaurant, for almost a decade before it became Centro.

stories.headline: Italian steakhouse seeks tax break to open in former Tavern Littleton
stories.summary:
Chachi's Italian-American plans to spend $2.8 million to open in February at 2589 W. Main St. in the former Tavern Littleton space. The Littleton City Council will discuss Tuesday whether the restaurant can keep half the sales tax revenue it generates, capped at $350,000 over five years.

Council documents say higher than anticipated costs, up to 30% because of economic conditions, have created a funding gap that risks depleting operating reserves. The discussion is part of a study session, and if members agree, a formal vote would be held Nov. 17.

Councilman Merrill Stillwell questioned what the city would gain and worried incentives could push up already high downtown rents. The owners, Rachel and Eric Hyatt, also own Grande Station nearby and describe Chachi's as a fine-dining steakhouse with handmade pasta.

stories.headline: Republicans criticize Democratic talk of changing voter-approved ballot measures
stories.summary:
House Republicans accused Democratic leaders of seeking to override voters after Gov.-elect Phil Weiser said some newly approved initiatives may need legislative adjustments. The measures include Propositions 132 and 133 on fentanyl and child sex trafficking, and 134 and 135 on transgender youth.

In a joint statement Monday, Republicans called on Weiser and the Democratic majority to respect the election outcome. Weiser said that when a statutory measure passes incomplete or not administrable, it is appropriate for the legislature to add adjustments. Propositions 134 and 135 passed with 52.19% and 51.92% of the vote.

Rep. Lorena Garcia, D-Adams County, said lawmakers and advocacy groups will explore options to limit the measures' impact, adding that nothing is off the table. Democrats now hold supermajorities and could amend the statutory measures by simple majority.

stories.headline: Early morning smash-and-grab hits several Douglas County businesses
stories.summary:
Suspects were caught on camera early Monday morning breaking into several Douglas County businesses, and investigators are asking the public for help.

No one is in custody. Anyone with information can contact Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-STOP.

stories.headline: One person hospitalized after downtown Denver shooting
stories.summary:
Denver police were investigating a shooting around 7:47 p.m. Monday in the 2100 block of Arapahoe Street in downtown Denver. One person was taken to a hospital.

No arrests have been made, and investigators are working to develop suspect information.

stories.headline: Lakewood police agent Nick Graham's memorial will be open to the public
stories.summary:
A public funeral for Lakewood Police Agent Nick Graham will be held at 10 a.m. Thursday at BRAVE Church, 3800 E. Hampden Ave., in Englewood, the Lakewood Police Department and Colorado Fallen Hero Foundation announced Monday. East Hampden Avenue will close between South Downing Street and South Colorado Boulevard starting at 7:30 a.m., with a blue tunnel of police cars from Downing to Monroe streets.

Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn, president of the foundation, encouraged residents to line the procession route with flags or hands over hearts. Lakewood police resumed regular patrols Monday after neighboring agencies covered the city while the department mourned.

Graham, 33, was killed Thursday when a parolee opened fire as agents boarded an RTD bus near Wadsworth Boulevard and West Colfax Avenue. Police identified the gunman, Gabriel Steven Garcia, 34, who was killed by return fire. Donations for Graham's family are being accepted.

stories.headline: Gov. Polis tours Catalyst Campus expansion in Colorado Springs
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis toured the Catalyst Campus for Technology and Innovation in Colorado Springs on Monday, where a 15,000-square-foot expansion is underway. The campus has expanded to train 700 people for aerospace and defense jobs.

The visit is among Polis's final duties in office, as he is term limited. He will leave office in January, when Governor-elect Phil Weiser is sworn in.

topStory.headline: Hegseth to Face Reporters as Massie Forces House Impeachment Vote Over Iran War
topStory.summary:
Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor Monday afternoon. Massie alleges Hegseth violated the Constitution by engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization. The articles also accuse Hegseth of abusing his power and endangering military personnel, including through the conduct of other operations such as lethal strikes on boats the administration says were smuggling drugs. Because Massie filed the measure as privileged under House rules, Republican leaders must act on it within two legislative days.

Hegseth has called the effort a "sham" and described Massie as a "disgruntled, defeated congressman." In a video statement last week, he said, "They attack us because we are effective," and added, "We will not back down." He scheduled a news conference at the Pentagon for 8 a.m. Tuesday to address the matter. President Trump has said he will stand by Hegseth, calling him "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country" on social media and urging Congress to "stand up for Pete!!!" Trump has also praised Hegseth's role in the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year.

The House could vote as early as 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, according to the daily floor schedule, which lists a procedural motion relating to the resolution. A Republican could move to table the measure or refer it to committee; either would require a majority and, if successful, would prevent a direct vote on impeachment. If such a motion fails, the House must vote on the resolution itself, which also takes a majority. Attendance may matter, as 36 House members were absent for votes Monday night. Massie said he does not know whether the measure has the votes to advance, and NBC News reported that no Republican other than Massie has publicly committed to supporting it. The New York Times reported that Democrats are widely expected to back the charges and that as few as three Republican defections or absences could let them advance.

The move comes after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections, though they remain in power until January. Massie, who lost a primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger and is retiring at the end of his term, has criticized Trump and the Iran war since it began nearly nine months ago. He first introduced impeachment articles in September and says the renewed effort is a "much gentler version" of what Democrats would pursue next year, with the aim of pressuring Trump to name a replacement who could be confirmed while Republicans still control the Senate. Democratic leaders have signaled openness to pursuing impeachment once they take control in January. House Speaker Mike Johnson has announced he will not seek the minority leader post, and House and Senate Republicans are selecting new leadership teams Tuesday.

Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, a Senate trial would require a two-thirds vote to convict and remove him, a high threshold, and party leaders could delay any trial. Impeachments of cabinet-level officials are rare, and a House vote advancing the charges would signal bipartisan opposition in Congress. The Defense Department's record $1.5 trillion budget request remains pending, with some lawmakers citing Hegseth as one reason it has not been approved. The outcome of Tuesday's procedural vote will indicate how much Republican support Hegseth retains heading into a Democratic-controlled Congress.
